nameStory: Field mustard gets its name from exactly where you'd expect to find it - growing wild in agricultural fields and disturbed ground. The "mustard" part comes from its membership in the mustard family, whose seeds have been ground into the spicy yellow condiment we know and love for thousands of years.
description: Field mustard is a fast-growing annual plant that can reach 1-4 feet tall, with a branching stem topped by clusters of small, bright yellow flowers. This weedy cousin of turnips and bok choy has deeply lobed lower leaves that feel somewhat rough to the touch, and smaller, simpler leaves higher up the stem. It's a hardy pioneer plant that quickly colonizes disturbed soil, producing slender seed pods that rattle when mature.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Bright yellow flowers with exactly four petals arranged in a cross shape - a hallmark of the mustard family. Each tiny flower is about 1/4 inch across and clusters together at the stem tips, creating cheerful yellow bouquets that smell faintly sweet.

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Lower leaves are deeply lobed and feel slightly rough like fine sandpaper, while upper leaves are smaller and less divided. The leaves alternate up the stem and have a slightly bitter, peppery taste when chewed.

idTips.label: Fruit/Seeds
idTips.description: Long, thin seed pods called siliques that stand upright and parallel to the stem. When ripe, they turn brown and make a soft rattling sound when shaken, splitting open to release tiny round seeds.

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Grows as a single-stemmed plant that branches near the top, creating an inverted triangle shape. The main stem feels sturdy but hollow when pinched, and the whole plant has a somewhat weedy, opportunistic appearance.

habitat: Look for field mustard in disturbed soils like farm fields, roadsides, vacant lots, and construction sites throughout New England. It thrives in sunny locations with rich, loose soil but is adaptable enough to grow in compacted ground and even cracks in pavement. This opportunistic plant often appears alongside other weedy species like dandelions and plantain.

seasonality.spring: Young plants emerge early and can be found as low rosettes of deeply lobed leaves. The tender young leaves are actually edible and have a mild mustard flavor.
seasonality.summer: Peak blooming time, with bright yellow flower clusters at their showiest from June through August. This is when the distinctive four-petaled cross-shaped flowers are most visible.
seasonality.fall: Flowers give way to upright seed pods that turn from green to brown. Late-season plants may still be blooming while earlier ones are already setting seed.
seasonality.winter: Annual plants die back completely, but seeds remain dormant in the soil, ready to sprout when warm weather returns.

funFact: This humble weed is actually the wild ancestor of some of our most beloved vegetables - turnips, bok choy, napa cabbage, and even rapini all evolved from field mustard through thousands of years of selective breeding by farmers across Asia and Europe.
confusionNotes: Most easily confused with other yellow-flowered mustard family plants, but field mustard's upright seed pods that hug the stem are distinctive. Wild radish has similar flowers but produces fat, segmented seed pods that stick out from the stem like stubby fingers.
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called "field mustard," the table mustard in your refrigerator typically comes from brown mustard (Brassica juncea) or white mustard (Sinapis alba), not this species. However, field mustard seeds were historically used to make mustard condiment and can still be ground up for a spicy seasoning.
compareHints: Field mustard is smaller and weedier-looking than its cultivated cousins like cabbage and broccoli, but shares their four-petaled yellow flowers (though cabbage family crops are usually harvested before flowering). Unlike brown mustard, field mustard has seed pods that press close to the stem rather than spreading outward, and its lower leaves are more deeply lobed than those of rapeseed.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Unlike its relatives field mustard and brown mustard, wild cabbage has distinctively thick, waxy, blue-green leaves rather than thin, bright green ones.
Brown mustard differs from its close relative field mustard by having more deeply divided, darker leaves and a taller, more robust growth habit.
Compared to field mustard, rapeseed is much taller and more robust with thicker stems and larger flower clusters.
